21.0.0.en: The return journey of Paul and his companions to Jerusalem began. After they left Miletus and bade farewell to the priests of Ephesus and the believers there, they headed to the island of Cos and from it to the island of Rhodes in the Mediterranean Sea, and reached the port of Patara in southern Turkey.

21.1.0.en: After that they boarded a ship heading for Phoenicia (present-day Lebanon).

21.2.0.en: As they crossed the sea, they saw Cyprus on their left from afar. And they sailed to Tyre, the most important port of Phoenicia, so that the ship might unload its cargo before continuing its voyage.

21.3.0.en: Through the Spirit: the Holy Spirit revealed to some of the prophets among the believers of Tyre that Paul would meet persecutions and dangers in Jerusalem.

21.3.1.en: During their stay in Tyre they visited the Christians there for seven days, the time for the ship to unload its cargo. The believers were telling Paul not to go to Jerusalem, because the Holy Spirit had informed them that he would meet troubles in it. This was not a divine declaration forbidding him to travel there, but only a disclosure of the persecutions he would meet.

21.4.0.en: At the end of the seven days, when the ship was ready to sail, all accompanied him on his way, and they knelt and prayed together on the shore. The hearts of all were attached to him, for the men, women and children came to bid him farewell after spending seven days with him.

21.5.0.en: After bidding Paul farewell, the people of Tyre returned to their homes, and he and his companions completed their journey.

21.5.1.en: If problems appear on the path of your spiritual life or your ministry, do not be disturbed or turn back from walking with God, as long as the Holy Spirit within you guides you to continue, confirmed by your father of confession and your guides. Christ will support you, and you will experience Him more deeply than you feel Him in ordinary times.

21.6.0.en: Then they came by sea from Tyre to Ptolemais, that is, Acre, and greeted the Christians who were there and stayed with them one day.

21.7.0.en: Caesarea: a port on the Mediterranean Sea, seventy miles from Jerusalem.

21.7.1.en: Paul's companions travelled with him by land to Caesarea of Palestine, and stayed in the house of Philip the deacon, who baptized the Ethiopian eunuch and was one of the seven deacons (6:5-6).

21.8.0.en: Philip had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy.

21.9.0.en: Paul stayed with Philip a long time so as not to go to Jerusalem except at the feast of Pentecost, until a Christian prophet from Judea named Agabus came (ch. 10:27-30).

21.10.1.en: Agabus took Paul's girdle and bound his own hands and feet, and said by a declaration of the Holy Spirit that the man who owns this girdle, that is, Paul, would be bound by the Jews at Jerusalem and delivered into the hands of the Gentiles, that is, the Roman authority.

21.11.0.en: When Paul's friends heard this, they besought him, together with the people of Acre, not to go up to Jerusalem.

21.12.0.en: Paul declared to those around him that their pity for him pained him, for it was contrary to his feelings, which were readiness to endure sufferings and even death for the sake of Christ.

21.13.0.en: Paul's friends ceased from asking, submitting to the ordering of God.

21.14.0.en: After completing their stay in Caesarea, they made ready and travelled by land to Jerusalem, and some of the believers from Caesarea came with them, and they stayed in Jerusalem in the house of a Christian man of Cypriot origin named Mnason.

21.14.1.en: Be discerning of the words of those who pity you; if they hinder your spiritual life, do not listen to them, and thank them for their love.

21.15.0.en: Paul entered Jerusalem for the fifth time, and the believers in it rejoiced at meeting him.

21.16.0.en: Paul met with James the brother of the Lord, that is, the cousin of the Lord Christ, and bishop of Jerusalem, and all the priests of Jerusalem attended the meeting. Thus the third missionary journey came to an end.

21.17.0.en: Paul explained to those present the details of the Lord's work with him in the ministry to the Gentiles, and how many churches were founded in Europe, and the alms he had collected for the needy in the Church of Jerusalem.

21.18.0.en: Myriads: ten thousand, and what is meant is a great number.

21.18.1.en: Those present rejoiced and glorified God, and informed Paul that there were many Christians of Jewish origin who held fast to the Jewish law even after becoming Christians.

21.19.0.en: The false brethren distorted Paul's reputation. These were the converts of Jewish origin who proclaimed the necessity of becoming Jews before believing in Christ. The Jews who did not believe hated Paul, and the Jews who believed doubted him, so they spread the report that Paul teaches that no law-observance should be carried out and forbids circumcision. By this they stirred everyone up against him.

21.20.0.en: It was expected that the Jews, both converts and non-converts, would come to Jerusalem during the days of the feast of Pentecost, and of course they would meet Paul, of whom they had heard that he is against their law, so the Church thought of a way to calm their feelings against him.

21.21.0.en: Purify thyself with them: take part in fulfilling the Jewish law.

21.21.1.en: That they may shave their heads: the law of the Nazirite was that he should not shave his head except at the end of the period of the vow. To disprove the accusations directed against Paul, the members of the Church advised him to take with him four converted men who had vows upon them, and to spend on them from his own money as the well-to-do among the Jews do for the poor, so that they might shave their heads and offer the sacrifices required at the end of the vow, so that all would see his keeping of the Law and know the falsehood of the rumors against him.

21.22.0.en: They reassured Paul that they had told the Christians of Gentile origin not to keep anything of the Jewish law except abstaining from what is sacrificed to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from fornication. So what they asked of Paul was merely to calm the Jews who were in an uproar against him in Jerusalem, and it was not required of Christians in general throughout the world.

21.23.0.en: Paul obeyed and took the men and purified himself with them according to the Law, and notified the priests that one week remained to complete the period of the vow, so that they might prepare the required sacrifices.

21.24.0.en: When the remaining seven days of the period of the vow were about to end, which are the most important days of the vow, in which the worship and purifications are offered, the Jews who had come from the region of Ephesus in western Turkey stirred up the crowds against him and laid hands on him, crying out and calling for the help of the fanatical Jews, and claiming that Paul had brought pagan men into the temple to defile it and had not been careful to keep them in the court of the Gentiles. This is a charge that deserves death, because he had defiled the temple.

21.25.0.en: The Jews' accusation against Paul was not true, but was an inference of theirs, because they had seen with him in the city Trophimus the Ephesian, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.

21.26.0.en: All Jerusalem was moved, and the Jews hurried toward the temple and seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, then shut its doors, being careful that it should not be defiled.

21.27.0.en: The Jews beat Paul severely with the intent of killing him. Next to the temple was a fortress in which was a commander who led a cohort of 1,000 soldiers, named Claudius Lysias. When the news reached him from the Roman soldiers stationed next to the temple, he immediately took centurions with their soldiers, that is, no fewer than 300 soldiers, and ran down upon them, rushing through the crowds to put an end to the riot, and commanded them not to beat Paul.

21.27.1.en: How necessary it is for a person to be careful in his conclusions, lest he wrong others by supposing that what he has imagined is true. And how anger cancels the minds of men and makes their actions irrational and mad. So do not rush in your words and actions, and rely on prayer so that you do not wrong others when they are not at fault, and do not agree with those around you without thinking, for they may be mistaken.

21.28.s.en: (4) Paul in the custody of the Roman government

21.28.0.en: The commander came near to Paul and took him and bound him with two chains to two soldiers to guard him, and asked who he was and what he had done.

21.29.0.en: The commander could not understand anything because of the intensity of the uproar, so he commanded that Paul be taken into the fortress.

21.30.0.en: Away with him: take him away to be killed, that is, kill him without trial because he deserves it.

21.30.1.en: When they reached the stairs connecting the court of the temple with the fortress, the soldiers carried Paul to save him from the violence of the crowds who were following him, crying out and demanding his death.

21.31.0.en: When they were about to enter the fortress, Paul spoke to the commander in Greek, asking permission to speak with him. The commander was amazed at his knowledge of Greek, and felt that he was of a high degree of culture, for he had supposed him to be a Jew who knew only Aramaic or Hebrew, which is the language of the Jews.

21.32.0.en: An Egyptian had led a band of robbers and murderers to Jerusalem, and claimed to be a prophet, and the number of his followers reached thirty thousand. He persuaded them that if he stood with them on the Mount of Olives opposite Jerusalem and commanded the walls of Jerusalem to fall, they would fall, and he would lead them to plunder the city. Felix the governor fought them and killed four hundred of them and captured two hundred, then the Egyptian fled and his army was scattered in A.D. 54. The commander supposed that Paul was this man who was wanted for arrest.

21.33.0.en: Paul told him that he was a citizen of the well-known city of Tarsus, and that he was a Jew and not an Egyptian, but from the region of Cilicia, which is part of present-day Turkey, and asked him to permit him to address the crowds.

21.34.0.en: The commander permitted Paul, so he stood on the stairs and beckoned with his hand, and the people became completely quiet, and he began to address them in the Hebrew language to win their goodwill.

21.34.1.en: God sends to His children someone to deliver them at the right time from the hand of those who wrong them, and preserves their lives to complete their mission, as He did with Paul. So be reassured, continue your life in positive works, and do not worry about the threats of the wicked.

21.34.2.en: Paul's address to the Jews in the temple

22.0.s.en: (1) Paul's vision on the road to Damascus

22.0.0.en: Paul began his defense of himself by showing great respect to those who had beaten him, calling them brethren and fathers, pointing to his Jewish origin and his respect for his elders despite their wrong toward him, and he asked them to listen to his defense of himself.

22.1.0.en: Paul used the Hebrew language in his speech to win their sympathy, and he succeeded in making them silent to listen to him, because they thought he would address them in Greek, which they also understood, but he spoke in the national language to show his attachment to his Jewish life and to the Law, and so he attracted their attention and their listening.

22.2.0.en: At the feet: the custom anciently was for the teacher to sit on a seat and the disciples before him on the ground.

22.2.1.en: The perfect manner of the law: the study of the Law with all exactness.

22.2.2.en: Of the fathers: handed down from the fathers.

22.2.3.en: Zealous: holding fast to the law of God with zeal and care.

22.2.4.en: Paul began to tell of his former life as a Jew born in Tarsus in Turkey, but was sent to study the Law in Jerusalem, and became a disciple at the hands of Gamaliel, the famous Jewish teacher, whom everyone respected for the breadth of his understanding and the moderation of his thought, and who was one of the seventy elders of the highest council of the Jews, that is, the Sanhedrin. In Jerusalem he learned and trained to carry out the Law with all zeal and exactness.

22.3.0.en: Paul persecuted Christianity when it appeared, and Christianity was called "the Way," because its children considered it the way to reach God, and we do not forget the saying of the Lord Christ, "I am the way" (Jn 14:6). He used to seize the Christians, men and women, with all cruelty, and bind them and lead them to prison and death; indeed it was he who stood to keep the garments of those who stoned Stephen.

22.4.0.en: Paul called to witness the high priest and the members of the highest council, because they had previously given him letters to the synagogue of the Jews in Damascus, so that he might seize those of the Jews who had become Christians and bring them to Jerusalem to be tried and punished.

22.5.0.en: Paul declared the reason for his change from persecuting Christianity to believing in it, which was a divine revelation to him from heaven. While he was on the way to Damascus, a vision appeared to him at noon, in which he saw a great light.

22.6.0.en: Paul fell to the ground and heard the voice of Christ rebuking him because of his persecution of Him, for his persecution of the Christians is a persecution of Christ Himself.

22.7.0.en: When Paul asked the speaker who He was, He answered that He is Jesus Christ whom Paul was persecuting.

22.8.0.en: Those who were with Paul, of the Jews, testify that they saw the light and were afraid, but although they heard the voice they did not understand the words.

22.8.1.en: And we notice that there is no real difference between what Paul mentioned here and what is mentioned in the same book in the ninth chapter in the description of the vision. Of those with Paul it was said that they heard the voice and saw no one, that is, they heard a sound without understanding the words clearly and in detail. And they saw the light but did not distinguish in it a particular person, and this agrees with what is stated here. So there is no difference between the two texts.

22.9.0.en: Christ asked Paul to enter Damascus, where God had arranged for him what he would do for the rest of his life.

22.10.0.en: Since he lost his sight for a temporary period because of the brightness of the light, his companions led him the rest of the way to Damascus.

22.10.1.en: If you sin unintentionally, God's grace does not reject you but guides you to repentance and return to Him. So be obedient to the voice of God, and you will enjoy His care and He will be glorified in you and through you.

22.11.0.en: Paul told that Ananias, a man exact in keeping the Law and whose piety all testify to, a Jew who had become a Christian and indeed had become a priest, came and prayed, and his sight returned to him at once.

22.12.0.en: That thou shouldest know his will: the Christian teachings and the salvation that Christ accomplished on the Cross. That Just One: Christ.

22.12.1.en: Of his mouth: the direct teachings from Christ in his solitude with Him for three years in the wilderness. The Apostle declared that Christ had chosen him to see Him and hear His voice, therefore the Church considers Paul an apostle like the twelve apostles, because he heard the call from the Lord and spoke with Him as they did, when he was alone with Him three years in the wilderness (Gal 1:17-18).

22.13.0.en: After this vision and his solitude with Christ in the wilderness, Paul was to witness for Him and preach Him among the Jews and the Gentiles.

22.14.0.en: Ananias asked Paul to hasten to receive Baptism for the forgiveness of his sins. This shows that Baptism is a sacrament of the Church and not ordinary water, because it forgives sins. He also asked him to pray, calling on the name of Christ as God, for the rite of Baptism includes the declaration of faith in Christ by the one being baptized.

22.14.1.en: It is a great grace to know Christ and be joined to the Church. So take care to deepen your knowledge of God in His Church and submit to His will which He declares to you in His Holy Book and at the hand of your father of confession. And take care to teach and draw others to enjoy with you the fellowship of God in the Church.

22.15.s.en: (3) Paul's vision in the temple and the agitation of the Jews against him

22.15.0.en: Paul returned from Damascus to Jerusalem after about three years that he spent in the Arabian desert adjoining Damascus, in which he received the faith from Christ Himself as an apostle (1 Cor 11:23). While he was praying in the temple, he fell into a trance. He declares here that his becoming a Christian had not removed him from praying in the temple or from holding fast to the promises of God to the fathers and their teachings, so as to win the Jews and his hearers when they see that he is still like them.

22.16.0.en: He saw Christ in a vision, asking him to leave Jerusalem quickly, since its people would not receive his testimony.

22.17.0.en: Paul thought that his past, which they knew, in his persecution of Christianity, would be a motive for them to accept his testimony, and especially his part in the killing of Stephen, the chief of the deacons and the first martyr, and his complete consent to that killing by keeping the garments of those who stoned him. If he was so great a persecutor of Christianity, then his change and conviction of it must have been for strong and convincing reasons, which would make the Jews accept his words and be affected by them.

22.18.0.en: Christ sent Paul to preach among the Gentiles, far from Jerusalem and the nation of the Jews. This means that Paul's preaching to the Gentiles is a divine command and is not against the Jews nor a neglect of the teaching of the fathers.

22.19.0.en: Here the Jews were greatly enraged because he considered the Gentiles better than themselves, and they demanded of the commander that he be killed, since they believed that salvation is for the Jews only and despised the Gentiles, and did not understand the prophecies of the prophets about the faith of the Gentiles and their salvation.

22.20.0.en: The Jews began to shout, expressing the intensity of their anger against him, and cast off their clothes and threw them down as if preparing to stone him, so that they would not hinder the movement of their hands in stoning. And they threw dust into the air instead of throwing stones at Paul, since the commander prevented them from that, and they did not know that they were rejecting the opportunity of their believing through Paul's preaching, which perhaps was the last, just as they had earlier rejected the visitation of Christ to Jerusalem when He wept over it (Lk 19:41).

22.21.0.en: The commander ordered the speech to be ended and that he be taken into the fortress and tortured by beating, so that he might confess what evil he had done that made the Jews hate him so, especially since the commander did not know the Hebrew language in which Paul had delivered his speech.

22.21.1.en: It is good for a person to discern the voice of God and not reject it as these did, for this may be the last opportunity for repentance, and after it comes hardness of heart through sin. So examine yourself by every word God sends you and review yourself every day before you sleep, so that if you have rushed into anger or contempt and rejected the word of God, you may return and submit to it and repent.

22.22.0.en: When they bound Paul in preparation for scourging him, he said to the centurion whom the commander had charged with supervising that, that he was a Roman by nationality and it was not permitted to scourge him. So the centurion hurried and told the commander this, because whoever scourges a Roman is punished by death according to Roman law.

22.23.0.en: The commander came at once to Paul, and made sure from him personally that he was a Roman, since the punishment of one who claims this falsely is death; and he marvelled that he had this privilege, for he had supposed him to be an ordinary Jew.

22.24.0.en: The commander told Paul that he had bought this rank, since the Caesars used to sell it and it was a source of great income to them, and asked Paul how he obtained the honor of this citizenship, and Paul declared that he had it by inheritance from his father and his forefathers, and this is considered a higher degree than that which is purchased.

22.25.0.en: The commander was afraid at once because he had been hasty in binding Paul for scourging, and he removed from him those who were about to scourge him.

22.26.0.en: The next day the commander ordered the chief priests and the council of the Sanhedrin to be gathered, and brought Paul down from the fortress to the council, and Paul stood to be tried before the council of which he had been a member, and the commander himself attended to know what Paul had done.

22.26.1.en: It is your right to defend yourself and use your means, but let it be for the glory of God and not for personal purposes. At the same time, do not be disturbed if you find no opportunity to defend yourself. And accept sufferings for the sake of Christ, taking care that you are not at fault in anything, that is, that you suffer while innocent, and thus you will have the heavenly reward.

22.26.2.en: Paul's address in the Sanhedrin, the plot of the Jews, and his transfer to Caesarea
